the adverb πανδημὶ indicates the extent of the action
εὐδοκία means goodwill, and ὅπλῳ is an instrumental dative
ζῆλος is a noun meaning zeal or enthusiasm
ῥητορεία is a noun meaning the art of speaking or rhetoric

The whole earth should celebrate the festival of Stephen; for he cultivated the entire world with words in succession and filled the whole inhabited world with holy laws; he sowed everywhere the doctrines of piety, and gave to all the churches the light of his teaching; just as the sun rising from one corner of the heaven illuminates the whole visible creation, so Stephen, flashing from Jerusalem, filled all cities and regions, nations and peoples, tribes and languages with unextinguished theology; we owe him more festivals, since he is a citizen of the Cross, a native of Bethlehem, a descendant of the Resurrection, a table-server of Zion, a herald of the Ascension; he pitched his tents and tabernacles among us; among us he received the lot and portion of ministry and martyrdom; here he has the altar of sacrifice and the step of blessing, the field of teaching and the theater of rhetoric; from here he was taken up into the heavens and departed to Christ; therefore we often have festivals in his honor, and frequently crown him with a wreath, and continually ascend the wine-press, singing a wedding song and a song of the wine-press

Lord, you crowned us with the armor of goodwill. For the faithful, Stephen's zeal is a weapon, and the tongue is a sword for the pious, and the boldness of confession is a preparation, and courage is an encouragement, and rhetoric is the material of theology, and teaching is the catechesis of the law, and knowledge of the prophets, and understanding of the Gospels, and the contemplation of heavenly, or rather superheavenly, mysteries is an explanation. But who is able to speak of Stephen's virtues? What shall I call him? Martyr of light, servant of life, soldier of Christ, lamp of the Word, pearl of the Spirit, flower of endurance, foundation of philosophy, example of apathy, firstfruits of teachers, pillar of the church, educator of grace, ladder of virtues, pillar of progress, forerunner of the apostles, firstborn of martyrs, leader of knowledge. He was a deacon, but he ordained himself for the churches. He was appointed to bring in bread, but he brought in contrary doctrines. He changed the tables into altars. He used the bread from heaven, not from earth. He transferred the cup of drunkenness to the cups of grace. Instead of wine, he poured out the Spirit, and instead of sensible water, he brought forth the mystical and intelligible. He was much spoken and doing, teaching and working wonders, convicting Jews, casting out demons, healing the sicknesses of both body and soul. He opened his mouth, and all hearing was hunted. He stretched out his tongue, and death fled, falsehood was bound, and love progressed. Being a lamb, he fought against the wolves on behalf of the shepherd.

Being stronger, he subjected dragons to the eagle; he provided the character of an angel by being silent to those judging; he laughed, seeing the informers circling; and seeing the false witnesses standing by, he said these things to himself from David's lyre playing: 'The blows of children have become their blows'; for whatever the informer shoots, the worker of truth is not wounded; whatever arrows the evil one releases, he moves and sends in vain; for he does not wound the upright, does not strike the innocent, does not bite the blameless; what kind of thing was the appearance of slander? 'This man does not cease speaking words against this holy place and the law'; 'this man'; who? 'the one performing wonders and signs beyond human capability; the one drawing the whole spring of wisdom; the one emptying the treasuries of grace into himself'
pass_b_english: The whole earth should celebrate the festival of Stephen, for he has cultivated the entire world with his words and filled it with holy laws. He has sowed the doctrines of piety everywhere, giving all the churches the light of his teaching. Just as the sun rises from one corner of the heaven and illuminates the whole visible creation, so Stephen, flashing from Jerusalem, has filled all cities and regions, nations and peoples, tribes and languages with unextinguished theology.

We owe Stephen more festivals, since he is a citizen of the Cross, a native of Bethlehem, a descendant of the Resurrection, a table-server of Zion, and a herald of the Ascension. He has pitched his tents and tabernacles among us, and among us he has received the lot and portion of ministry and martyrdom. Here he has the altar of sacrifice and the step of blessing, the field of teaching and the theater of rhetoric. From here he was taken up into the heavens and departed to Christ.

The Lord has crowned us with the armor of goodwill, and for the faithful, Stephen's zeal is a powerful weapon. His tongue is a sword that cuts through falsehood, and his boldness in confession is a preparation for the battles of life. The courage that fills his heart is an encouragement to all who follow him, and his rhetoric is the material of theology, shaping the minds of those who listen. As a teacher, he imparts the catechesis of the law, and his knowledge of the prophets and the Gospels is unparalleled. He contemplates the mysteries of heaven and the superheavenly realm, and his explanation of these mysteries is a gift to all who hear him.

But who can speak of Stephen's virtues? What title can we give him? He is the martyr of light, the servant of life, the soldier of Christ, the lamp of the Word, the pearl of the Spirit. He is the flower of endurance, the foundation of philosophy, the example of apathy, the firstfruits of teachers, the pillar of the church, the educator of grace, the ladder of virtues, the pillar of progress. He is the forerunner of the apostles, the firstborn of martyrs, the leader of knowledge. As a deacon, he ordained himself for the churches, and he brought in contrary doctrines instead of bread. He changed the tables into altars and used the bread from heaven, not from earth. He transferred the cup of drunkenness to the cups of grace, pouring out the Spirit instead of wine, and bringing forth the mystical and intelligible instead of sensible water.

He was a man of great words and deeds, teaching and working wonders, convicting Jews, casting out demons, and healing the sicknesses of both body and soul. With his mouth open, he hunted down all hearing, and with his tongue stretched out, death fled, falsehood was bound, and love progressed. Like a lamb, he fought against the wolves on behalf of the shepherd.

In his strength, he subjugated the dragons to the eagle, and by his silence, he presented the character of an angel to those who judged him. He laughed as he saw the informers circling, and seeing the false witnesses standing by, he said these things to himself from David's lyre playing: 'The blows of children have become their blows'.

Whatever the informer shoots, the worker of truth is not wounded; whatever arrows the evil one releases, he moves and sends in vain; for he does not wound the upright, does not strike the innocent, does not bite the blameless.

λυχνίαν τοῦ Λόγου, μαργαρίτην τοῦ Πνεύματος, ὑπομονῆς ἄνθος, φιλοσοφίας
